meaning: Based on how things look right now, the speaker judges that something is unlikely to happen. Like “doesn't look like ...” or “I'm afraid ... won't ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + そうもない／そうにない／そうにもない

senses.label: Doesn't look like ...
senses.meaning: The negative of 「〜そうだ」 (appearance). Judging from what they can see, the speaker thinks something probably won't happen. Often used for objective situations like the weather or progress.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうもない (e.g. 「降りそうもない」, 「止みそうにない」)
examples: This rain doesn't look like it'll stop anytime soon.
The sky is bright, so it doesn't look like it'll rain.

senses.label: I'm afraid I can't ...
senses.meaning: With potential verbs or 「できる」, it says the speaker probably can't do something or won't make it in time. Often has a tone of regret, or “there's nothing I can do”.
senses.connection: Potential verb masu-stem + そうもない (e.g. 「間に合いそうもない」, 「行けそうにない」)
examples: I'm afraid it won't be finished today.
Sorry, I don't think I can make it to the party tomorrow.
This much food? There's no way I can eat it all.

notes: 「そうもない」 sounds slightly stronger than 「そうにない」. 「そうにもない」 stresses “no matter how you look at it, it won't happen”.
Adjectives don't use this form. Instead of 「✕高そうもない」, say 「高くなさそうだ」 or 「高そうではない」.
Often used with adverbs like 「とても」, 「なかなか」, 「当分」, and 「到底」.

daily.title: Waiting for the bus
daily.description: The bus just won't come, so you grumble to a friend.
daily.example: Doesn't look like the bus is coming anytime soon. Shall we walk?

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: A friend invites you out on the weekend, but you probably can't go.
daily.example: I have work this weekend, so I don't think I can go.

daily.title: Checking the weather
daily.description: Looking out the window before leaving in the morning.
daily.example: It doesn't look like it'll clear up today, so I'll take an umbrella.

work.title: Reporting a delay
work.description: Telling your boss you won't finish by the deadline.
work.example: I'm very sorry, but I don't think we'll make the deadline.

work.title: Assessing a negotiation
work.description: Discussing the outlook with a coworker after a meeting.
work.example: On their terms, it doesn't look like we'll reach an agreement.

etymology: Made from 「〜そうだ」 (appearance) plus 「も」 (emphasis) or 「に」 (the continuative form of 「そうだ」), then 「ない」. Literally “there isn't even that look”, which came to mean “doesn't look like it will ...”.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: 「降りそうだ」 means “looks like it'll rain”. 「降りそうもない」 is its negative: “doesn't look like it'll rain”.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: 「はずがない」 rules something out based on reasoning or logic, and sounds very certain. 「そうもない」 is a guess from what you see, so it's weaker.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 「〜ないかもしれない」 just means “maybe not”, about 50/50. 「そうもない」 leans toward “almost certainly not”.

meaning: Something (usually unwanted) is about to happen. The past form 「〜そうになった」 often means “almost ...” or “nearly ...”.

senses.label: Almost ...
senses.meaning: 「〜そうになった」 means something nearly happened but didn't. Usually something unwanted, like falling, crying, or forgetting. Often paired with 「危うく」 or 「もう少しで」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうになった (e.g. 「転びそうになった」, 「泣きそうになった」)
examples: I almost slipped and fell many times on the snowy road.
I nearly cried at the end of the movie.
I almost forgot an important appointment.

senses.label: About to ...
senses.meaning: Something is on the verge of happening. The present form often describes something that keeps happening. Often followed by 「〜て」, 「〜たら」, or 「〜のを」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうになる／そうになって／そうになったら
examples: I'm so sleepy my eyes keep closing in class.
When you feel like giving up, remember these words.

senses.label: Holding back ...
senses.meaning: 「〜そうになるのを＋こらえる／我慢する」 means barely holding back a reaction that's about to come out. Mostly for emotions like laughing, crying, or getting angry.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうになるのを + こらえる／我慢する
examples: I tried desperately not to burst out laughing.

notes: The subject is usually an involuntary action or change, not a deliberate one. For “about to (deliberately) do”, use 「〜ようとする」.
「〜そうになった」 only means “almost”: it didn't actually happen. If it did happen, use 「〜てしまった」.
With adjectives, as in 「おいしそうになる」, it means “come to look ...”. That's different from the “almost” meaning here.

daily.title: A close call
daily.description: Telling your family about a near accident today.
daily.example: I almost got hit by a bicycle. It really scared me!

daily.title: Talking about a moving film
daily.description: Sharing impressions with a friend after a movie.
daily.example: That last scene almost brought me to tears.

daily.title: Nearly missing your stop
daily.description: Telling a friend you fell asleep on the train.
daily.example: I fell asleep and almost missed my station.

work.title: Reporting a near miss
work.description: Reporting a mistake that almost happened, in a meeting.
work.example: Because I didn't double-check, I almost sent the wrong data.

work.title: Talking about a past project
work.description: Describing difficulties in a project during a job interview.
work.example: I almost gave up many times along the way, but I saw it through to the end.

etymology: Made from 「そうに」, the continuative form of 「〜そうだ」 (appearance), plus the verb 「なる」. Literally “come to look like it will ...”, which led to “about to ...” and “almost ...”.

similar.title: 〜ところだった
similar.explanation: Both can mean “almost”. 「ところだった」 follows the dictionary form and is often used for serious near misses, often with relief. 「そうになった」 focuses more on your body or emotions being about to lose control.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとする
similar.explanation: 「ようとする」 is deliberately trying to do something. 「そうになる」 is something about to happen on its own.

similar.title: 〜かける
similar.explanation: 「かける」 means the action has already partly started (「死にかける」). 「そうになる」 means it hasn't started yet; it's just about to.

meaning: Trying to do something, or an action or change that is about to happen. Like “try to ...” or “be about to ...”.

senses.label: Try to ...
senses.meaning: Making an effort to achieve something. Often hints that it isn't going well, or describes someone else's actions.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + とする／としている (e.g. 「覚えようとする」, 「説明しようとした」)
examples: He was desperately trying to tell us something.
Even when I try to remember, the name won't come to me.
My son is trying to solve the problem on his own.

senses.label: Just as I was about to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ようとした時／ところ」 means that just as you were about to do something, something else happened. The second half is usually a surprise or an interruption.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + とした時／とした瞬間／としたところ
examples: Just as I was about to leave the house, the phone rang.
Just as I was about to get on the train, the doors closed.

senses.label: Is about to ...
senses.meaning: With a non-living subject or time as the subject, it shows a change is just about to happen. Has a written, descriptive feel.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb, volitional form + としている (e.g. 「日が沈もうとしている」)
examples: The evening sun is about to set.
The long winter is coming to an end.

notes: To state your own plans, use 「〜ようと思う」. You don't say 「✕私は来年留学しようとする」.
The negative 「〜ようとしない」 means “refuse to ...”. See that entry.
「〜ようとしても〜ない」 (“even if I try, I can't ...”) is a common pattern.

daily.title: Telling a funny story
daily.description: Describing to a friend what your cat did.
daily.example: The cat tried to jump onto a high shelf and failed.

daily.title: Complaining about noise
daily.description: Telling your family you got disturbed just as you were going to sleep.
daily.example: Just as I was going to sleep, the next room got noisy.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A scene in a novel describing the change of seasons.
daily.example: Summer was coming to an end.

work.title: Explaining a system error
work.description: Telling tech support when the problem happens.
work.example: When I try to save the file, an error appears.

work.title: News report
work.description: A news commentary on the progress of a reform.
work.example: The government is trying to introduce a new system.

etymology: Made from the verb volitional form 「〜(よ)う」, the quoting particle 「と」, and 「する」. Literally “act toward ‘let's do it’”, which led to “try to” and “be about to”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: 「ようと思う」 states the speaker's own plan, which stays in their head. 「ようとする」 means already starting to act, or being about to.

similar.title: 〜るところだ
similar.explanation: 「るところだ」 simply describes the moment “just about to”. 「ようとする」 adds a sense of intention and effort.

similar.title: 〜そうになる
similar.explanation: 「そうになる」 is something about to happen on its own. 「ようとする」 is a conscious attempt (it only means “about to” with a non-volitional subject).

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとしない
similar.explanation: The negative of this pattern: “refuse to, won't even try to”. Often used to criticize others.

meaning: Someone refuses to do something or has no will to do it. Mostly used about a third person, showing the speaker's frustration or resignation.
connection: Verb volitional form + としない

senses.label: Won't / refuse to
senses.meaning: No matter how much others urge or wait, the person won't do it. Mostly used in the third person. Often sounds annoyed or impatient.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + としない／としなかった (e.g. 「聞こうとしない」, 「認めようとしない」)
examples: He never admits his mistakes.
My child just won't eat vegetables.
No matter how many times I warned him, my subordinate wouldn't change the way he worked.

senses.label: Won't even ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ようともしない」 and 「〜ようとはしない」 add 「も」 or 「は」 to stress that not even a minimal attempt is made. The frustration is stronger.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + ともしない／とはしない
examples: My son won't even listen to me.
She made no attempt to explain why.

notes: Usually not used about yourself. To say you have no intention of doing something, use 「〜つもりはない」.
Things can also be the subject, meaning “just won't ...”, as in 「ドアが開こうとしない」. This sounds like personification.
The polite form is 「〜ようとしません」. 「〜ようとしないんです」 is also common when complaining.

daily.title: Complaining about your kid
daily.description: A mother complains to a friend that her child won't study.
daily.example: My kid just won't study at all.

daily.title: A stubborn parent
daily.description: Talking with your brother about your dad refusing to see a doctor.
daily.example: Dad won't go to the hospital. I'm worried.

daily.title: Caring for a pet
daily.description: Explaining to the vet that your dog won't eat.
daily.example: He hasn't wanted to eat since yesterday.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: The news criticizes a company's attitude.
work.example: The company refuses to admit responsibility, and criticism is growing.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Explaining that the client won't budge.
work.example: They won't agree to negotiate on price.

etymology: The negative of 「〜(よ)うとする」 (try to). Literally “not even having the intention to do”, so it means “refuse to”. In writing, 「〜ようとせず」 is used to link clauses.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとする
similar.explanation: The positive form of this pattern: “try to, be about to”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うにも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ようにも〜ない」 means “want to but can't”: the will is there, but circumstances prevent it. 「ようとしない」 means not wanting to at all.

similar.title: 〜つもりはない
similar.explanation: 「つもりはない」 is mostly about the speaker's own lack of intention. 「ようとしない」 mostly describes others who refuse.

meaning: There is no way or means to do something, so it can't be done even if you want to. Like “there's no way to ...”.

senses.label: No way to ...
senses.meaning: There's no method, clue, or condition that makes it possible. It's not that you don't want to; you simply can't. Often sounds resigned.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ようがない／ようもない (e.g. 「連絡しようがない」, 「直しようがない」)
examples: I don't know their address or phone number, so there's no way to contact them.
Once it's this broken, there's no way to fix it.
If we don't know the cause, there's no way to come up with a solution.

senses.label: Beyond words
senses.meaning: 「言いようがない」, 「例えようがない」, etc. describe something so extreme that words can't express it. Often used for strong feelings.
senses.connection: 言い／例え／表し + ようがない (often as 「〜としか言いようがない」)
examples: The beauty of that scenery is beyond compare.
That can only be called a miracle.

senses.label: Before a noun
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「〜ようのない」: “that can't be ...”. Common in writing and literature.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ようのない + noun (e.g. 「言いようのない不安」)
examples: I felt a loneliness I couldn't describe.

notes: It can follow a noun as 「Nのしようがない」: 「返事のしようがない」 (“there's no way to reply”).
「しようがない」 has the same origin as casual 「しょうがない」, which also means “it can't be helped”.
Don't confuse it with the volitional 「〜よう」: 「書きようがない」 uses the masu-stem, not 「✕書こうがない」.

daily.title: Losing something
daily.description: Telling a friend you lost something and don't know where to look.
daily.example: I don't know where I dropped it, so there's no way to look for it.

daily.title: Asked something you don't know
daily.description: A friend asks about something you never heard about.
daily.example: Nobody told me, so how am I supposed to answer?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's complicated feelings.
daily.example: She was wrapped in an anxiety she couldn't put into words.

work.title: Replying to a client
work.description: There isn't enough information to give a quote.
work.example: Without detailed specifications, we are unable to provide a quote.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting that an accident investigation has stalled.
work.example: No records remain, so there is no way to confirm it.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」 and means “way, manner”. 「〜ようがない」 literally means “there is no way of ...”. In this meaning it's usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うにも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ようにも〜ない」 follows the volitional form and stresses the feeling “I want to, but I can't”. 「ようがない」 follows the masu-stem and stresses “there are no means”.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 「かねる」 means “find it hard to, given my position”, often in polite refusals. 「ようがない」 means there's objectively no way.

similar.title: 〜ても仕方がない
similar.explanation: 「ても仕方がない」 means “there's no point even if you do it”: possible but pointless. 「ようがない」 means it simply can't be done.

meaning: Based on reason, duty, or common sense, something ought to be done. Like “should ...” or “ought to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べきだ (「する」 often becomes 「すべきだ」)

senses.label: Should ...
senses.meaning: Something ought to be done according to reason, responsibility, or social norms. It's the speaker's own judgment or opinion. Stronger and more formal than 「〜ほうがいい」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べきだ／べきです (e.g. 「謝るべきだ」, 「守るべきだ」)
examples: You should keep your promises.
If you think you were wrong, you should apologize right away.
I think we should discuss this issue more.

senses.label: Should have ...
senses.meaning: 「〜べきだった」 means something should have been done in the past but wasn't. About yourself, it shows regret; about others, it's criticism.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べきだった
examples: I should have gone to the doctor sooner.
I should have told the truth back then.

senses.label: べき + noun
senses.meaning: 「〜べき + noun」 modifies a noun directly: “that should be ...”, “worth ...”. Very common in writing.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べき + noun (e.g. 「やるべきこと」, 「読むべき本」)
examples: First, let's make a list of what needs to be done today.
This is a book every student should read.

notes: With 「する」, both 「するべき」 and 「すべき」 are fine; 「すべき」 is more formal.
The negative is 「〜べきではない」. You don't say 「✕〜ないべきだ」.
It's not used for duties set by laws or rules; use 「〜なければならない」 for those. 「べき」 is a judgment based on reason.
Saying 「〜べきです」 directly to a superior sounds pushy. Try 「〜たほうがいいと思います」 instead.

daily.title: Advising a friend
daily.description: Your friend had a fight with their partner, and you give advice.
daily.example: You should be the one to reach out first.

daily.title: Forgot an umbrella
daily.description: Talking to yourself when it starts raining.
daily.example: I knew I should have brought an umbrella.

daily.title: Talking about society
daily.description: Discussing the news with family.
daily.example: We should be kinder to older people.

work.title: Making a point in a meeting
work.description: Stating your opinion in a meeting.
work.example: I believe we should listen to our customers first.

work.title: Editorial
work.description: A newspaper editorial makes demands about policy.
work.example: The government should take action immediately.

etymology: 「べき」 is the attributive form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 「べし」 expressed things like naturalness, duty, and conjecture; modern Japanese mainly keeps the sense of “ought to”.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is softer advice. 「べきだ」 is an opinion based on principle, stronger and more preachy.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 「なければならない」 usually refers to rules or objective necessity. 「べきだ」 is what the speaker thinks is right in principle.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「はずだ」 is a logical guess: “should be (as expected)”. 「べきだ」 is a claim: “ought to do”.

similar.title: 〜ことだ (advice)
similar.explanation: 「ことだ」 is personal advice to a specific person. 「べきだ」 mostly expresses general principles and opinions.

meaning: Based on reason, morals, or common sense, something should not be done. Like “shouldn't ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べきではない (「する」 often becomes 「すべきではない」)

senses.label: Shouldn't ...
senses.meaning: Something shouldn't be done according to reason or morals. Fairly strong; often used to discourage, criticize, or state an opinion.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べきではない／べきではありません／べきじゃない
examples: You shouldn't speak badly of others.
You shouldn't give up so easily.
Children shouldn't be shown movies like this.

senses.label: Shouldn't have ...
senses.meaning: 「〜べきではなかった」 means something was done in the past that shouldn't have been. About yourself, it shows regret; about others, it's criticism.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べきではなかった
examples: I shouldn't have said something like that.
I really shouldn't have bought that stock.

senses.label: Shouldn't we ...?
senses.meaning: 「〜べきではないか」 and 「〜べきではないでしょうか」 make a point softly as a rhetorical question. They actually mean “we should ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べきではないか／べきではないでしょうか
examples: Shouldn't we listen more to what young people have to say?

notes: You can't say 「✕〜ないべきだ」. The negative is always 「〜べきではない」.
In writing, 「〜べきでない」 (without 「は」) is also common.
「べきではないか」 looks negative, but it's actually a positive claim. Don't misread it.

daily.title: Warning a friend
daily.description: Your friend wants to stay up late playing games, and you tell them not to.
daily.example: You've got an exam tomorrow. You shouldn't stay up late.

daily.title: Regretting overeating
daily.description: Talking to yourself after an all-you-can-eat buffet.
daily.example: I shouldn't have eaten that much.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Giving your opinion on an online controversy.
daily.example: People shouldn't post other people's private information online.

work.title: Meeting discussion
work.description: Opposing a hasty decision.
work.example: We shouldn't make a decision without enough data.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A newspaper column criticizes a certain approach.
work.example: Decisions shouldn't be made on economic grounds alone.

etymology: The negative of 「べきだ」 (「べき」, the attributive form of 「べし」, + 「だ」). It means “it's not something that ought to be done”.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: The positive form of this pattern: “should ...”.

similar.title: 〜ものではない
similar.explanation: 「ものではない」 is advice based on social norms, “(generally) one shouldn't ...”, and often sounds preachy. 「べきではない」 is more the speaker's own opinion and judgment.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: 「てはいけない」 is a clear prohibition, often about rules. 「べきではない」 is “shouldn't” in principle; it isn't necessarily forbidden.

similar.title: 〜べからず
similar.explanation: 「べからず」 is an old-style prohibition seen on signs and in sayings, as in 「芝生に入るべからず」 (“Keep off the grass”).

title: 〜ことだ (advice)
meaning: Used to give advice: “you'd better ...”, “the best thing is to ...”. Usually sounds like an older person talking to a younger one, or a boss to a subordinate.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことだ

senses.label: The best thing is to ...
senses.meaning: The speaker thinks this is the best thing to do. It's quite direct, with a feel of “take my word for it”. Often used as 「〜たければ〜ことだ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことだ／ことです (e.g. 「休むことだ」, 「練習することだ」)
examples: If you want to get over your cold quickly, get plenty of rest.
If you want to get better at it, practice every day.
If there's something you don't understand, ask your teacher right away.

senses.label: Better not ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ないことだ」 advises the listener not to do something. Often used for warnings.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ことだ (e.g. 「無理をしないことだ」)
examples: For your health, don't push yourself too hard.
Don't be quick to believe rumors.

notes: Mostly used from older to younger, or from boss to subordinate. Using it to a superior or a customer is rude.
Don't confuse it with plain statements like 「大切なのは〜ことだ」. This pattern is advice to a specific person.
「〜ということだ」 expresses hearsay or a conclusion. It's a different pattern.

daily.title: A parent's advice
daily.description: A parent advises a child before an exam.
daily.example: The day before an exam, you'd better go to bed early.

daily.title: Tips from a senior student
daily.description: An older student shares tips on learning a language.
daily.example: If you want to get good at Japanese, the key is just to talk.

daily.title: Looking out for a friend
daily.description: Your friend has been tired lately, so you tell them to take it easy.
daily.example: When you're tired, don't push yourself.

work.title: Coaching a new hire
work.description: A boss gives work advice to a new employee.
work.example: If you make a mistake, the first thing to do is report it right away.

work.title: Advice column
work.description: A magazine column gives advice to readers.
work.example: If you're thinking about changing jobs, start by knowing your strengths.

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」 and the copula 「だ」. Literally “the (thing to do) is ...”, which came to point out the best course of action.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is general advice for anyone. 「ことだ」 sounds more like guidance from a senior, and is more direct.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: 「べきだ」 stresses what's right in principle and can state general opinions. 「ことだ」 is advice to a specific person in a specific situation.

similar.title: 〜ものだ (common sense)
similar.explanation: 「ものだ」 talks about social norms: “that's how it should be”. 「ことだ」 is personal advice suited to the listener's situation.

title: 〜こと (instructions / rules)
meaning: Placed at the end of a sentence in rules, notices, and instructions to show something that must be followed. Like “must ...” or “... is required”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + こと (at the end of a sentence)

senses.label: Must ... (instruction)
senses.meaning: Used in written rules, notices, and assignment instructions to tell the reader to do something. Short, commanding, and neutral in tone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + こと。(e.g. 「提出すること」, 「記入すること」)
examples: Reports must be submitted by Friday.
Names must be written in ballpoint pen.

senses.label: Do not ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ないこと」 expresses a prohibition. Common on signs, in school rules, and in exam instructions.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + こと。(e.g. 「走らないこと」)
examples: No running in the hallways.
Dictionaries may not be used during the exam.

notes: Only used in written rules, notices, or a teacher's assignment instructions. Not for requests in everyday conversation.
Often appears as a list item, followed directly by 「。」 or a line break.
When giving instructions out loud, use 「〜てください」 or 「〜ないでください」 instead.

daily.title: Reading apartment rules
daily.description: Reading your building's trash rules after moving in.
daily.example: Trash must be put out by 8 a.m.

daily.title: Homework instructions
daily.description: The teacher writes the homework instructions on the board.
daily.example: Homework must be done before the next class.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: A note in the employee handbook.
work.example: Confidential documents must not be taken out of the office.

work.title: Exam rules
work.description: Instructions for people taking a certification exam.
work.example: Do not leave the room during the first 30 minutes of the exam.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 at the end of a sentence, with something like 「〜ことになっている」 or 「〜ことを求める」 left out. It means “the thing to do is ...”, and became a written instruction or rule.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 「てください」 is a polite spoken request. Sentence-final 「こと」 is a written rule with no politeness.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: 「なさい」 is a spoken command, often from parents or teachers. 「こと」 mostly appears in written rules.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: 「ことになっている」 explains “that's the rule”. Sentence-final 「こと」 states the rule itself.

meaning: There's no need to do something. Often used to comfort or encourage someone. Like “there's no need to ...” or “you don't have to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ことはない

senses.label: No need to ...
senses.meaning: There's no need to do it. Often used to reassure or encourage, with a “don't worry” tone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことはない／ことはありません (e.g. 「心配することはない」)
examples: There's no need to worry so much.
There's no need to come all this way. An email is enough.
You don't need to apologize. It's my fault.

senses.label: Didn't need to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ことはなかった」 means it wasn't actually necessary to do it. Often implies wasted effort or mild blame.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことはなかった
examples: We didn't need to rush like that.
There was no need to cry at all.

senses.label: Will never ...
senses.meaning: States that something will never happen, ruling out the possibility. Often paired with 「決して」 or 「二度と」. Mostly written.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことはない (often with 「決して」 or 「二度と」)
examples: I'll probably never forget that day.
This bridge won't collapse, even in an earthquake.

notes: Ta-form + 「ことはない」 means “have never ...” (experience), as in 「行ったことはない」. That's a different pattern.
「〜こともない」 is also used. It's slightly softer: “there's no need to ... either”.
Saying 「〜ことはありません」 to a superior can sound rude. Try 「〜なくても大丈夫です」 instead.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is down after failing an exam.
daily.example: You failed once, that's all. No need to be so down.

daily.title: Politely declining
daily.description: A friend offers to walk you to the station.
daily.example: You don't have to walk me to the station. I can get home on my own.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: You lined up for ages, but it wasn't crowded at all.
daily.example: We didn't need to line up this early.

work.title: Reassuring a subordinate
work.description: A boss talks to a subordinate who made a small mistake.
work.example: A mistake this small isn't worth worrying about.

work.title: Explaining safety
work.description: Telling a customer the product is safe.
work.example: It will not break down under normal use.

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」, the topic particle 「は」, and 「ない」. Literally “there is no (doing) that”, which came to mean “no need to” and “won't happen”.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: 「なくてもいい」 just states objectively that you don't have to. 「ことはない」 adds feeling, reassuring or encouraging the listener.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: 「たことはない」 means “have never ...” (experience). Dictionary form + 「ことはない」 means “no need to”. The connections are different.

similar.title: 〜ないことはない
similar.explanation: 「ないことはない」 is a double negative: “it's not that ... not”. It means something completely different from 「ことはない」.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: 「には及ばない」 also means “no need to”, but it's more formal and polite. 「ことはない」 is common in speech.

meaning: A double negative meaning “it's not that ... not”. Something is possible to some extent, but the speaker is unenthusiastic or reluctant. Like “I could, I suppose”.
connection: Verb / adjective nai-form + ことはない／こともない; nai-form without い + くはない

senses.label: It's not that ... not
senses.meaning: Admits that something is possible or true, but without enthusiasm. Often followed by 「けど」 or 「が」 to add a reservation or condition. Vaguer and softer than a plain yes.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective nai-form + ことはない／こともない (e.g. 「できないことはない」, 「行けないこともない」)
examples: If I take my time, it's not impossible.
It's not that I can't eat spicy food.
I could go, I guess, but it's a bit far.

senses.label: なくはない
senses.meaning: 「〜なくはない」 and 「〜なくもない」 are shorter ways of saying the same thing. Often used to softly show understanding or agreement.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective nai-form without い + くはない／くもない (e.g. 「わからなくはない」, 「賛成できなくもない」)
examples: I can sort of understand why he's angry.
Depending on the terms, I might be able to agree.

notes: It looks like 「〜ことはない」 (no need to), but the meaning is very different: 「心配することはない」 is “no need to worry”, while 「心配しないことはない」 is “it's not that I'm not worried”.
The tone is unenthusiastic and vague. Useful when you don't want to clearly refuse or clearly agree.
「も」 is softer than 「は」, with more of a “sort of, I guess” feel.

daily.title: Asked if you can cook
daily.description: A friend asks if you cook, and you answer modestly.
daily.example: I can cook, sort of, but I'm not very good.

daily.title: Unsure about going
daily.description: A friend invites you hiking on the weekend.
daily.example: I might go. Depends on the weather.

daily.title: Showing understanding
daily.description: After hearing a friend's complaints, you show some sympathy.
daily.example: Well, I can kind of see how you feel.

work.title: Answering your boss
work.description: Your boss asks if you can finish early, and you hint it'll be tough.
work.example: If I work overtime, I think I could probably make it.

work.title: Leaving room to negotiate
work.description: Telling a client their proposal is open to discussion.
work.example: Depending on the quantity, a discount may not be out of the question.

etymology: Made from the negative 「ない」, the formal noun 「こと」, and 「はない」. Literally “there's no case of not ...”. The two negatives cancel out, giving a cautious yes.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: Dictionary form + 「ことはない」 means “no need to”. Nai-form + 「ことはない」 is a double negative, “it's not that ... not”. Both the connection and the meaning differ.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「わけではない」 is a partial negation: “it's not (entirely) that ...”. 「ないことはない」 starts from the negative side and admits “it's possible”.

similar.title: 〜ないものでもない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, but 「ないものでもない」 is more formal and stiff. It's N1 level.

meaning: Repeats the same word to admit a fact, then uses 「が」 or 「けど」 to add a reservation or complaint. Like “it is ..., but ...” or “I did ..., but ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form + ことは + same word + が／けど

senses.label: I did, but ...
senses.meaning: Admits that an action was done or can be done, but the result or degree isn't satisfying. The same verb is repeated, and the second half contrasts.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + ことは + same verb + が／けど (e.g. 「行くことは行ったが」)
examples: I did go to the party, but I left right away.
I did read that book, but I don't remember much of it.
I can speak Japanese, sure, but I'm not good at keigo.

senses.label: It is ..., but ...
senses.meaning: With adjectives, it admits a quality but also points out a drawback. Often used to evaluate things or places.
senses.connection: i-adjective plain form / na-adjective + な + ことは + same word + が／けど (e.g. 「おいしいことはおいしいけど」, 「便利なことは便利だが」)
examples: The ramen here is good, sure, but it's a bit pricey.
An apartment near the station is convenient, sure, but it's noisy.

notes: The same word must be repeated. For the past, the second word takes the past form: both 「行くことは行った」 and 「行ったことは行った」 are fine.
Na-adjectives take 「な」 before and 「だ」 after: 「静かなことは静かだ」.
The second half is usually a reservation, complaint, or extra detail. It can't be a further positive point.

daily.title: Reviewing a new purchase
daily.description: Talking about your new phone with a friend.
daily.example: It's light, sure, but the battery dies fast.

daily.title: Asked about homework
daily.description: Your mom asks if you've done your homework.
daily.example: I did do it, but I'm only halfway through.

daily.title: Travel impressions
daily.description: Telling a coworker about a place you visited.
daily.example: It was beautiful, sure, but there were way too many people.

work.title: Progress report
work.description: Telling your boss about contacting a client.
work.example: I did contact them, but I haven't heard back yet.

work.title: Evaluating a plan
work.description: Commenting on a new proposal in a meeting.
work.example: This plan is cheap, yes, but I have concerns about the quality.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 plus the topic particle 「は」 raises an action or quality as the topic. The same word then confirms it, and the conjunction 「が」 turns to a contrast.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「ものの」 also means “although ...”, but it's written style and doesn't repeat a word. 「ことは〜が」 is common in speech and feels like a grudging admission.

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: 「といっても」 stresses that the actual degree is lower than you'd think. 「ことは〜が」 stresses “it really is ..., but there's a drawback”.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「わけではない」 denies someone's inference. 「ことは〜が」 first admits something, then adds a reservation.

meaning: Something set by rules, custom, or someone else's decision that stays in effect. Like “the rule is that ...” or “it's been arranged that ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになっている

senses.label: The rule is ...
senses.meaning: Describes rules such as laws, school rules, or company policy. It's not something the speaker decided. Often used to explain rules to others.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになっている／ことになっています
examples: In this dorm, you're not allowed to go out after 11 p.m.
When you take a day off, you're supposed to call in by 9 a.m.
In Japan, cars drive on the left.

senses.label: Fixed plans
senses.meaning: Plans that have already been agreed or set. Usually decided by a group or someone else, and you follow them.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことになっている (e.g. 「会うことになっている」)
examples: I'm meeting a friend at the station at ten tomorrow.
I'm set to start working at the Osaka branch next month.

senses.label: Was supposed to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ことになっていた」 describes the original plan. Often followed by 「が」 or 「のに」 to say the plan fell through.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことになっていた + が／のに
examples: We were supposed to leave today, but it was postponed because of the typhoon.

notes: 「ことになる」 means “it's been decided / it turned out”, focusing on the change. 「ことになっている」 focuses on the ongoing rule or arrangement.
For habits you decided on yourself, use 「〜ことにしている」.
In formal situations, say 「〜ことになっております」.

daily.title: Explaining house rules
daily.description: Explaining the trash rules to a new roommate.
daily.example: Here, burnable trash goes out on Tuesdays.

daily.title: Explaining your schedule
daily.description: A friend asks you out for the weekend, but you already have plans.
daily.example: On Saturday, my family and I are going to a hot spring.

work.title: Explaining rules to a visitor
work.description: A receptionist explains company rules to a visitor.
work.example: Visitors are given an entry pass at reception.

work.title: Confirming meeting roles
work.description: Confirming meeting arrangements with a coworker.
work.example: Junior staff are the ones who take the meeting minutes.

work.title: Explaining contract terms
work.description: Explaining a contract clause to a client.
work.example: Cancellations must be requested at least one month in advance.

etymology: Made from 「〜ことになる」 (something gets decided) plus 「〜ている」 for an ongoing state. Literally “being in a decided state”, so it expresses rules and plans.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: 「ことになる」 reports the change “it's been decided that ...”, often as news. 「ことになっている」 is an established rule or arrangement that stays in effect.

similar.title: 〜ことにしている
similar.explanation: 「ことにしている」 is a habit you decided on and stick to. 「ことになっている」 is a rule set from outside or by others.

similar.title: 〜ようになっている
similar.explanation: 「ようになっている」 explains how a machine or system is designed to work. 「ことになっている」 explains rules set by people.

meaning: A habit or principle you decided on yourself and stick to. Like “I make a point of ...” or “I always ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことにしている

senses.label: Make a point of ...
senses.meaning: You chose to do something and have kept doing it, so it's now a habit. Mostly used in the first person.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことにしている／ことにしています
examples: For my health, I make a point of walking for 30 minutes every morning.
I make it a habit to write in my diary before bed.
I always spend weekends with my family.

senses.label: Make a point of not ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ないことにしている」 means you've set yourself a rule not to do something.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ことにしている
examples: I make it a rule not to eat anything after 9 p.m.
I make a point of not talking about work at home.

notes: 「ことにする」 is deciding right now. 「ことにしている」 is the ongoing state after deciding.
Use 「〜ことになっている」 for outside rules and 「〜ことにしている」 for your own decisions. Don't mix them up.
「〜たことにしておく」 means “let's just say ...”. That's a different usage.

daily.title: Healthy habits
daily.description: A friend asks how you stay in shape.
daily.example: I don't use elevators. I always take the stairs.

daily.title: Talking about money
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about saving.
daily.example: When I get paid, I always put away 10,000 yen first.

daily.title: Turning down a loan
daily.description: Politely refusing a friend who wants to borrow money.
daily.example: Sorry, but I make it a rule not to lend money to friends.

work.title: Job interview
work.description: Describing your work habits to an interviewer.
work.example: I make a point of always organizing my work by the end of each day.

work.title: Explaining your policy
work.description: Explaining how you work to a client.
work.example: We make it our policy to always send important notices in writing.

etymology: Made from 「〜ことにする」 (decide to do) plus 「〜ている」 for an ongoing state. Literally “being in the state of having decided to do”, so it expresses a self-imposed habit.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: 「ことにする」 is the moment of deciding. 「ことにしている」 is the long-term habit after deciding.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: 「ことになっている」 is a rule set by others. 「ことにしている」 is set by yourself.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: 「ようにする」 means “try to”, stressing effort. 「ことにしている」 is a clear rule you've set, followed more firmly.

meaning: Uses a fact as the basis or cause for a result, a judgment, or the origin of a name. Like “since ...”, “judging from ...”, or “because ...”. Written style.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + である + ことから

senses.label: Because ...
senses.meaning: Gives an objective cause or reason. Often used to explain social trends or how events unfolded. Objective in tone; common in news and explanatory writing.
senses.connection: Plain form + ことから (na-adjectives: 「〜なことから」; nouns: 「〜であることから」)
examples: Because it's close to the station, this town is popular with young people.
Because there has been little rain this year, there are worries about a water shortage.

senses.label: Origin of a name
senses.meaning: Explains where a name comes from. The second half is often 「〜と呼ばれる」 or 「〜と名付けられた」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ことから + 「〜」と呼ばれる／名付けられた
examples: This slope is called Sakurazaka (“Cherry Blossom Slope”) because many cherry trees used to bloom here.
Because its shape resembles Mt. Fuji, this mountain was named Kofuji (“Little Fuji”).

senses.label: Judging from ...
senses.meaning: Draws a conclusion from an observed fact. The second half is often 「〜とわかる」, 「〜と考えられる」, or 「〜と見られる」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ことから + 〜とわかる／〜と考えられる
examples: Since the window was broken, the police believe a burglar got in.
From the wet road, you can tell it rained during the night.

notes: Quite formal and written. In everyday conversation, use 「〜から」 or 「〜ので」.
The second half can't be a command, request, or intention, e.g. 「✕近いことから、行こう」.
In 「できることから始める」, 「から」 means “start from”. That's not this pattern.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on population changes in a town.
daily.example: Thanks to strong support for raising children, more young families are moving here.

daily.title: Reading a sign while traveling
daily.description: Reading about the origin of a place name at a tourist spot.
daily.example: This bridge is called Meganebashi (“Spectacles Bridge”) because its shape looks like a pair of glasses.

work.title: Writing a research report
work.description: Explaining the basis for a conclusion in a report.
work.example: The sharp rise in inquiries shows strong interest in the new product.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Explaining the evidence for an inference in a paper.
work.example: Since the same pottery has been found in both regions, it is thought that they were in contact.

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」 and the particle 「から」, which marks a starting point or basis. Literally “starting from the fact that ...”, which led to the meanings of cause, basis, and origin.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: 「から」 can give subjective reasons and can be followed by commands or intentions. 「ことから」 is only for objective facts and is written style.

similar.title: 〜ことで
similar.explanation: 「ことで」 means “by ...” (means or cause), focusing on how a result came about. 「ことから」 focuses on the fact as evidence or origin.

similar.title: 〜から見ると
similar.explanation: 「から見ると」 shows the viewpoint or angle of a judgment. 「ことから」 bases the judgment on a specific fact.
